points.t: A painless crusted nodule or ulcer with a rolled edge on exposed skin, not healing after weeks of antibiotics, after travel or migration.
*Leishmania* parasites inoculated by sandfly bites, multiplying in dermal macrophages.
Refer to tropical medicine for confirmation (biopsy, PCR) and species-guided treatment; many Old World lesions heal on their own.
Mucosal leishmaniasis (New World species) and visceral disease in the immunosuppressed.

points: Some regions have an animal reservoir (rodents, dogs, sloths). *L. tropica* and *L. donovani* can pass human to human via sandflies.
Transmission is by **vector bite**. Spread by blood transfusion, needle-sharing and congenital routes is rare. CL is **not** spread by casual contact.
Incubation is usually **2 weeks to 6 months** and sometimes longer, so ask about travel well before the lesion appeared.
It sits on **exposed sites**: face, ears, forearms, hands and lower legs. There may be one lesion or several (several bites).
It is usually **painless**, and the patient is otherwise well (as in Case 1). Pain usually means secondary bacterial infection.
**Sporotrichoid spread** (nodules in a line along the lymphatics) and regional lymphadenopathy can occur, especially with *Viannia* species.
**Healing:** spontaneous healing over 2 months to more than a year leaves an **atrophic, cribriform, "cigarette-paper" scar**.
**Mucosal red flags** (New World, sometimes years later) are nasal stuffiness, nosebleeds, crusting, septal perforation, lip/palate ulcers and hoarseness.
comes from the travel/residence history plus a chronic, non-healing, painless ulcer or nodule on exposed skin (DermNet, PCDS).
because New World *Viannia* infection needs systemic treatment and ENT/mucosal examination.
In New World cases, check for mucosal involvement with **ENT/nasal examination**. If visceral disease is suspected (fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias), do FBC, LFTs and serology.
Serology is not useful for CL. It is used for visceral disease.

cards.name: Insect-bite reaction / infected bite
cards.clue: Acute, itchy or painful, resolves in days–weeks; no rolled indurated edge

cards.name: Ecthyma / bacterial ulcer (Strep/Staph)
cards.clue: Painful, purulent, quicker evolution; responds to antibiotics. Can co-exist as a secondary infection

cards.name: Basal cell / squamous cell carcinoma
cards.clue: Older patient, sun-exposed site, pearly or keratotic edge, slowly progressive; biopsy

cards.name: Atypical mycobacteria (M. marinum, M. ulcerans/Buruli)
cards.clue: Fish-tank or water exposure (*M. marinum*, sporotrichoid); Buruli = undermined painless ulcer, Africa/Australia

cards.name: Sporotrichosis / deep fungal infection
cards.clue: Gardening or thorn injury, sporotrichoid nodules; culture

cards.name: Pyoderma gangrenosum
cards.clue: Painful, rapidly enlarging, undermined violaceous edge, pathergy; associated IBD/arthritis

cards.name: Myiasis / tungiasis
cards.clue: Central punctum with larva/flea; very recent travel

cards.name: Granuloma annulare, sarcoidosis, chondrodermatitis (ear)
cards.clue: Non-ulcerating or typical sites; no travel link

items.t: Nasal stuffiness, bleeding or oral or nasal ulceration months or years later: **mucosal leishmaniasis**, specialist referral.
Immunosuppression or HIV: specialist advice early.

pearls.t: **Healing of the skin lesion does not exclude New World mucosal disease.** Advise patients to report nasal or oral symptoms even years later.
Lesions are **not contagious person to person**. Scarring is common, so set expectations and note the psychological impact of facial scars.
